meta.title: ACC Mock Exam — Set 2
meta.description: 60 scenario-based questions on the 2025 ICF Core Competencies, coaching boundaries, and Code of Ethics.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: An organization sponsors coaching for a senior director. Two months later, the CEO calls the coach asking whether the director plans to remain with the company. How MUST the coach respond?

options.text: Promise to ask the director for permission to send the CEO a brief update.
Decline to share coaching impressions and invite the CEO to speak with the director.
Confirm only that the director seems engaged, without revealing specific topics discussed in sessions.
Provide an objective summary of the director's commitment since the company sponsors the coaching.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance, Standards 2.1–2.2), which requires maintaining strict confidentiality with all parties unless disclosure has been explicitly agreed upon. Declining to disclose impressions and redirecting the CEO to speak directly with the director protects client privacy without creating organizational pressure. Option D is clearly wrong because paying for coaching does not grant a sponsor access to confidential assessments of the client. Both tricky distractors fail subtly: Option A sounds respectful of consent, yet offering to seek permission on the CEO's behalf places implicit organizational pressure on the director to waive privacy; Option C sounds harmless because it avoids specific topics, yet still leaks confidential impressions about the client's engagement.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client reports waking up with chest tightness and dread before work for two months and asks for coaching exercises to stop it. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Explore which specific workplace pressures seem tied to the client's morning distress.
Teach relaxation exercises and cognitive techniques to help eliminate the client's symptoms.
Validate their concern and ask what practical work changes might improve mornings.
Explain that physical symptoms exceed coaching scope and encourage consulting a healthcare professional.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice) and 2025 Code of Ethics Section 4 (Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value), which require recognizing the boundaries between coaching and clinical or medical care and referring when persistent physical or psychological distress arises. Two months of morning chest tightness and dread warrants evaluation by a qualified healthcare or mental health specialist. Option B is clearly wrong because prescribing symptom-relief interventions attempts to treat clinical or medical issues outside coaching scope. Both tricky distractors sound like supportive coaching: Option A uses exploratory questioning to investigate somatic symptoms instead of referring; Option C validates feelings and pivots to practical work changes, bypassing the ethical responsibility to encourage professional care first.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 7: Evokes Awareness
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client repeatedly postpones launching a freelance practice and asks, 'What do you think is really holding me back?' What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Ask what the client notices in themselves whenever they consider launching the practice.
Ask whether fear of financial uncertainty might be driving their repeated delays.
Acknowledge the pattern and ask what concrete step they can commit to tomorrow.
Offer a direct analysis of the main mindset barrier slowing down their launch.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 7 (Evokes Awareness), which emphasizes inviting self-reflection and insight through open-ended inquiry rather than supplying the coach's answers. Returning the inquiry to what the client notices internally supports client ownership and discovery. Option D is clearly wrong because offering a direct analysis diagnoses the barrier and positions the coach as an authority rather than evoking the client's own awareness. Both tricky distractors miss the mark subtly: Option B frames a leading hypothesis ('fear of financial uncertainty') as a closed question rather than letting the client name their own experience; Option C sounds action-oriented, yet rushes prematurely into Competency 8 action planning before the client explores what is underneath their hesitation.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 1: Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: HR signs and pays for a manager's coaching package, yet the manager arrives at Session 1 unfamiliar with the coaching agreement. What should the coach do?

options.text: Begin coaching immediately because HR's signed contract covers both the company and manager.
Hold Session 1 to build rapport and ask the manager to sign afterward.
Discuss and confirm the coaching agreement directly with the manager before coaching begins.
Confirm with HR that they briefed the manager on confidentiality and coaching expectations.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 1 (Agreements for Client and/or Sponsor Engagement, Standard 1.1) and Core Competency 3 (Establishes and Maintains Agreements). Before coaching begins, the coach must communicate directly with the client as well as the sponsor to co-create clarity around the nature of coaching, roles, confidentiality, and termination rights. Option A is clearly wrong because an organizational sponsor's signature does not establish the coachee's informed agreement. Both tricky distractors fail subtle requirements: Option B prioritizes rapport by deferring the agreement until after coaching starts, leaving confidentiality and boundaries unestablished during Session 1; Option D relies on HR as an intermediary instead of the coach ensuring direct mutual understanding with the client.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach works simultaneously with two rival regional directors in the same firm who occasionally mention each other during sessions. What is the BEST practice for the coach?

options.text: Keep each engagement completely confidential so neither director's discussions inform the other's coaching.
End one engagement promptly because coaching workplace rivals inherently compromises client confidentiality.
Ask each director's consent to share neutral themes that might ease regional tension.
Use background insights from one director's sessions privately to sharpen questions for the other.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance, Standards 2.1–2.2), which requires maintaining the strictest confidentiality across all parties and preventing any cross-pollination of private session data between clients in the same organization. Option D is clearly wrong because letting one client's confidential context shape questions for a rival directly breaches confidentiality firewalls. Both tricky distractors fail differently: Option B is a rigid over-correction, as ICF ethics do not prohibit coaching colleagues or competitors when confidentiality and potential conflicts are properly safeguarded; Option C sounds collaborative and consent-based, yet asking rival clients to cross-share themes compromises individual confidentiality boundaries and shifts the coach into organizational mediation.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach considers pasting anonymized session transcripts into a public generative AI tool to brainstorm stronger coaching questions. What should the coach do?

options.text: Proceed after removing names and company details, since anonymized text protects client confidentiality.
Upload the transcripts freely because material used solely for coach reflection requires no consent.
Summarize the client's dilemma briefly in the tool instead of pasting verbatim session dialogue.
Avoid uploading transcripts to public AI tools without verified privacy safeguards and client consent.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Standards 2.4 and 2.5 on Records Management and Technology/AI Systems), which hold coaches directly accountable for confidentiality, security, and informed consent across all digital tools and AI systems they use. Public generative AI tools may log or train on inputs and risk re-identification. Option B is clearly wrong because self-improvement or reflection never exempts a coach from privacy and consent duties. Both tricky distractors reflect common misconceptions: Option A assumes simple name removal guarantees anonymity even though full narratives remain identifiable in public tools; Option C substitutes a summary for a transcript, yet still exposes client data to an unvetted public AI system without privacy protections or informed consent.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client asks their coach to send coaching progress notes to their psychotherapist so both professionals remain aligned. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Decline the request because coordinating with a client's therapist blurs coaching and clinical boundaries.
Discuss confidentiality implications and obtain written consent defining what may be shared.
Offer to give the therapist an informal verbal update instead of sending written notes.
Forward all coaching notes promptly because the client verbally requested the disclosure.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance, Standard 2.2), which requires having a clear, explicit agreement—supported by written consent—about what information may be exchanged and how it is shared across involved parties. Discussing implications first protects the coaching space and ensures informed scope limits. Option D is clearly wrong because forwarding full session notes on a casual verbal request lacks documented authorization and clear scope boundaries. Both tricky distractors fall short: Option A is a rigid misapplication of boundaries, as communication with a clinician is permissible when clearly scoped and consented to in writing; Option C sounds cautious by avoiding written files, yet an informal phone update still shares confidential material without defined written scope.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach recommends a paid personality assessment from a vendor that pays the coach a referral fee per client. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Keep the financial arrangement private as long as the assessment genuinely benefits the client.
Stop recommending that vendor's assessment because receiving referral commissions violates coaching neutrality.
Disclose the referral commission clearly to clients before they decide to purchase the assessment.
Receive the referral benefit as free platform credits rather than direct cash compensation.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest, Standard 3.8), which mandates disclosing any compensation, referral fees, or benefits paid or received for referring clients to third-party products or services. Clear upfront disclosure preserves client autonomy and prevents hidden financial conflicts. Option A is clearly wrong because perceived usefulness does not excuse concealing a financial incentive. Both tricky distractors fail subtly: Option B is a rigid over-correction, since ICF allows recommending external tools with referral compensation provided it is transparently disclosed; Option D substitutes non-monetary platform credits for cash, yet ethical disclosure rules apply equally to both financial payments and non-cash benefits.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: During Session 4, a founder client invites their coach to become an angel investor in the startup. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Decline the investment offer and explain how a financial stake creates a conflict of interest.
Proceed only if both parties sign a written addendum acknowledging the potential financial conflict.
Invest modestly in the startup while promising to keep financial opinions out of sessions.
End the coaching engagement immediately because the client's invitation damaged professional boundaries.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest), which requires coaches to recognize and avoid dual relationships and financial conflicts that compromise objectivity and client-centered neutrality. Becoming an investor gives the coach a personal financial stake in the founder's business choices. Option C is clearly wrong because even a small equity stake creates an active conflict of interest regardless of promises to separate topics. Both tricky distractors fail subtly: Option B attempts a legalistic waiver, yet signing an addendum does not neutralize an ongoing investor-coachee power and objectivity conflict during active coaching; Option D over-corrects by abruptly terminating the entire coaching relationship when simply declining the offer protects boundaries.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach notices growing romantic attraction toward an active client who has recently begun making subtle personal compliments. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Express mutual interest gently and propose pausing coaching to explore dating each other.
Keep personal feelings private, redirect compliments toward goals, and continue coaching normally.
Disclose the romantic feelings candidly during the session to preserve complete emotional honesty.
Seek coaching supervision while maintaining firm boundaries, then address the shift or close.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest, Standard 3.6) and Core Competency 2 (Embodies a Coaching Mindset). ICF prohibits romantic or sexual involvement with active clients and requires taking appropriate action—including seeking supervision, maintaining boundaries, and addressing the issue or ending the engagement—when attraction emerges. Option A is clearly wrong because proposing to pause coaching to date an active client breaches romantic-boundary standards. Both tricky distractors sound conscientious yet fail: Option B sounds professional by keeping feelings private and redirecting to goals, yet ignoring a growing relational shift without supervision or boundary action violates Standard 3.6; Option C misapplies 'honesty' by confessing attraction in session, placing emotional burden on the client rather than safeguarding boundaries.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A startup founder brings an investor pitch deck to a session and asks the coach to identify the weakest slides. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Provide brief feedback on two slides first, then coach the founder on their reaction.
Explain that critiquing slides is consulting and ask where the founder feels least confident.
Ask the founder to put the deck away because coaching excludes reviewing workplace materials.
Review each slide carefully and list specific financial and narrative improvements for the founder.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice), which requires distinguishing coaching from consulting and maintaining role clarity. Evaluating slide quality and diagnosing flaws is expert consulting; redirecting to the founder's own confidence and discernment keeps ownership with the client. Option D is clearly wrong because analyzing slides and prescribing revisions steps directly into consulting. Both tricky distractors miss the boundary differently: Option A sounds accommodating by giving quick feedback on 'just two slides,' yet blends consulting into a coaching session without maintaining role clarity; Option C rigidly rejects the pitch deck altogether, overlooking that client materials can appropriately serve as prompts for the client's own self-evaluation.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client experiences nervousness and self-doubt ahead of an upcoming annual board vote and wants mental preparation support. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Draft the client's opening board remarks personally to reduce their pre-meeting performance pressure.
Clarify coaching's emotional boundaries and refer the client to a qualified therapist.
Explore what mindset and grounding perspective the client wants to bring into the meeting.
Ask why previous board meetings felt stressful so the client can unpack past fears.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice) and Competency 7 (Evokes Awareness). Situational nervousness and self-doubt before an important board vote is a normal human response, not a clinical condition; partnering with the client on their desired mindset and presence fits squarely within coaching. Option A is clearly wrong because writing the client's remarks turns the coach into a hands-on consultant doing the client's work. Both tricky distractors reflect common ACC exam traps: Option B uses boundary-sounding language to over-apply the therapy referral rule to ordinary situational nervousness; Option D asks a backward-looking 'why' question focused on unpacking past emotional fears rather than supporting forward-looking mental preparation.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Mentoring
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client transitioning from software engineering into people management asks the coach how to structure their first quarterly review. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Note that prescribing review structures is mentoring, then ask what outcomes the client wants.
Share a brief sample review outline first, then ask how the client might adapt it.
Ask whether starting with positive feedback before discussing development areas would make the review smoother.
Provide a proven quarterly review agenda from prior leadership experience and explain each step.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice), which requires distinguishing coaching from mentoring. Offering management playbooks or telling a new manager how to format reviews based on the coach's experience is mentoring; clarifying the boundary and exploring the client's desired outcomes keeps the session in coaching. Option D is clearly wrong because teaching a prior agenda directly substitutes mentoring for coaching. Both tricky distractors blend roles subtly: Option B tries a hybrid approach by offering a sample outline before asking questions, slipping into mentoring without separate agreement; Option C disguises a management prescription ('start with positive feedback first') as an open-sounding leading question.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Management
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: An executive asks their coach to join a live conflict meeting between two direct reports and mediate a resolution. How MUST the coach respond?

options.text: Meet privately with both direct reports beforehand to gather context for coaching the executive.
Join the meeting as mediator to help the executive and direct reports reach agreement.
Offer to facilitate the conflict as neutral team coaching if both direct reports agree.
Decline to mediate and explore how the executive wants to lead the conflict conversation.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice) and 2025 Code of Ethics Section 3 (Conflicts of Interest). Stepping into a live conflict among direct reports shifts the coach into managerial/HR mediation and compromises role clarity and neutrality; declining mediation while coaching the executive preserves client leadership ownership. Option B is clearly wrong because acting as a workplace mediator crosses out of coaching into direct management intervention. Both tricky distractors blur boundaries subtly: Option A pulls the coach into private fact-finding interviews with subordinates, creating dual-party confidentiality hazards; Option C tries to rebrand conflict mediation as 'neutral team coaching' despite an active individual coaching relationship and inherent boss-subordinate power asymmetries.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Friendship
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach and client live in the same neighborhood and occasionally meet at weekend gatherings, where the client raises session topics. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Terminate the coaching engagement because living in the same neighborhood creates a dual relationship.
Greet the client warmly while reserving all coaching topics for scheduled sessions.
Listen empathetically at the gathering without asking coaching questions so privacy stays intact.
Discuss the client's coaching update briefly over coffee to maintain rapport between scheduled sessions.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice) and 2025 Code of Ethics Sections 1–3 (Agreements, Confidentiality, and Dual Relationships). Casual social interactions require clear boundaries to distinguish coaching from friendship and protect confidentiality in public settings; warmly deferring coaching matters to scheduled sessions and clarifying expectations upholds both rapport and ethics. Option D is clearly wrong because holding informal coaching chats at social gatherings compromises confidentiality and professional boundaries. Both tricky distractors miss the balance: Option A over-corrects by terminating an engagement merely due to shared geography; Option C feels polite, yet passively listening to private coaching topics at a party still risks bystanders overhearing and blurs social versus coaching roles.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Medical Advice
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client experiencing afternoon fatigue asks whether intermittent fasting or supplements have helped the coach's other clients. How MUST the coach respond?

options.text: Share which supplements other clients found helpful while clarifying that results vary by individual.
Avoid mentioning other clients and ask how trying intermittent fasting might fit their schedule.
Decline to advise on fasting or supplements and encourage consulting a qualified healthcare professional.
Offer neutral published articles on fasting and fatigue so the client can decide independently.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice) and 2025 Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality) and Section 4 (Delivering Consistent Value). Recommending dietary regimens or supplements for physical fatigue falls into medical or nutritional advice outside coaching scope, and discussing other clients' outcomes risks breaching confidentiality. Option A is clearly wrong because it implicitly endorses supplements and reveals patterns from other clients. Both tricky distractors sound safer yet cross boundaries: Option B avoids naming other clients, yet uses a practical coaching question that implicitly steers the client toward trying intermittent fasting; Option D appears objective by supplying articles, yet curating health interventions for unassessed physical symptoms still encroaches on medical guidance.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Training
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client wants stronger negotiation outcomes and asks the coach to teach a structured negotiation framework during the session. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Explain that teaching frameworks is training and explore how the client currently approaches negotiations.
Teach a brief ten-minute framework summary first, then coach the client on applying it.
Walk through a proven five-step negotiation model and role-play each stage with the client.
Pause the coaching engagement until the client completes an external corporate negotiation training course.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice), which distinguishes coaching from training. Coaching helps clients develop awareness and self-generated strategies rather than delivering curriculum; clarifying the boundary and exploring the client's current approach keeps the session in coaching. Option C is clearly wrong because instructing and drilling a five-step model turns the coaching session into a training workshop. Both tricky distractors miss the mark subtly: Option B compromises role clarity by inserting a 'ten-minute' training segment inside coaching without keeping modalities distinct; Option D rigidly halts coaching altogether, overlooking that coaching can immediately explore mindset, preparation, and strategy alongside any optional external training.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 2: Embodies a Coaching Mindset
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: During a session, a client voices strong workplace policy views that clash sharply with the coach's personal values. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Terminate the coaching engagement immediately because differing personal values prevent authentic coaching support.
Challenge the client's policy stance directly using ethical arguments to broaden their social awareness.
Ask how the client's policy stance might negatively affect marginalized employees on their team.
Manage internal judgment, stay curious about the client's perspective, and reflect through supervision later.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 2 (Embodies a Coaching Mindset, including 2.07 maintaining emotional well-being, 2.09 nurturing openness and curiosity, and 2.10 monitoring how the coach's thoughts influence the client). Self-regulation in the moment combined with post-session reflection or supervision honors the client's agency while preventing coach bias from interfering. Option B is clearly wrong because debating the client with ethical arguments imposes the coach's personal values. Both tricky distractors fail subtly: Option A over-corrects by immediately ending coaching over a value difference before testing whether neutrality can be maintained; Option C disguises the coach's disapproval as a DEIB-focused 'how' question, steering the client rather than staying unattached and curious.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 3: Establishes and Maintains Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client opens Session 2 by saying, 'I want to talk about my co-founder,' and immediately recounts yesterday's argument. What should the coach do?

options.text: Listen quietly without interrupting until the client finishes describing the entire argument.
Acknowledge the situation and ask what they want to achieve around this topic today.
Reflect their concern and ask what conversation they want to schedule with their co-founder.
Interrupt immediately to explain conflict-resolution rules that co-founders should follow during disagreements.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 3 (Establishes and Maintains Agreements), which calls on the coach to partner with the client to define the session outcome and what makes the topic meaningful before diving deeply into narrative details. Option D is clearly wrong because cutting the client off to dispense conflict-resolution rules is directive and dismissive. Both tricky distractors sound like good coaching yet fail Competency 3: Option A confuses active listening with letting the client vent indefinitely without establishing a shared session focus; Option C acknowledges their concern yet jumps prematurely to Competency 8 action ('what conversation to schedule') before confirming what the client actually wants from today's session.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 8: Facilitates Client Growth
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Five minutes before Session 3 ends, an energized client lists six ambitious tasks to finish before next week. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Tell the client to drop four tasks immediately because six goals guarantee failure.
Validate their enthusiasm, record all six tasks, and wish them luck before next week.
Acknowledge their momentum and ask which priorities feel most realistic and actionable this week.
Offer to email daily mid-week reminders so the client finishes every task on time.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 8 (Facilitates Client Growth, including 8.07 partnering to sustain progress and client-owned accountability). Inviting the client to evaluate realism and prioritize respects client autonomy while encouraging sustainable action design. Option A is clearly wrong because ordering the client to drop four tasks violates partnership and imposes the coach's limits. Both tricky distractors sound supportive yet miss Competency 8: Option B enthusiastically endorses an overloaded list without partnering on feasibility, obstacles, or accountability; Option D offers hands-on accountability by sending daily reminders, transferring ownership from the client to the coach.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 1: Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client repeatedly cancels sessions two hours beforehand and says enforcing the 24-hour cancellation policy feels rigid. How should the coach respond?

options.text: Eliminate the cancellation policy immediately so the client feels unrestricted in scheduling.
Waive the recent fees temporarily while exploring what makes scheduling feel difficult.
Enforce the original terms strictly and refuse to modify any logistical expectations.
Apply the agreed policy while inviting conversation about workable future scheduling terms.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 1 (Agreements for Client and/or Sponsor Engagement, Standard 1.1) and Core Competency 3 (3.12, revisiting agreements when necessary), the coach upholds transparent agreements while partnering around future needs. Option D is correct because it maintains accountability to existing cancellation terms while inviting a collaborative review of future scheduling arrangements. Option A is clearly wrong because unilaterally discarding an agreed policy undermines contractual integrity. Option B is a tricky distractor (diplomatic boundary erosion): waiving repeated late cancellations while exploring difficulties sounds empathetic, yet erodes established Section 1 boundaries. Option C is a tricky distractor (rigid over-correction): enforcing the agreement without willingness to revisit future logistics misses the partnering spirit of Competency 3.12.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Two years after coaching ended, a former client's prospective employer calls the coach for an informal character reference. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Decline to confirm or share information without the former client's prior authorization.
Confirm the past coaching occurred while withholding all personal session details.
Offer general positive character remarks without referencing any coaching discussions.
Share an honest character evaluation since the engagement ended years ago.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance, Standards 2.1–2.2), confidentiality obligations apply indefinitely even after coaching concludes. Option A is correct because the coach protects both the former client's identity and any related information unless explicit prior consent exists. Option D is clearly wrong because the passage of time does not extinguish confidentiality duties. Option B is a tricky distractor (diplomatic boundary erosion): withholding session topics sounds protective, yet merely confirming that someone was a coaching client breaches privacy without consent. Option C is a tricky distractor: offering positive remarks without citing sessions sounds helpful and harmless, yet still discloses confidential impressions from the professional relationship without authorization.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client accidentally posts confidential merger details in a group chat containing the coach and support staff. What should the coach do first?

options.text: Post in the group thread asking everyone present to delete the message.
Wait until the next session to review secure communication agreements with the client.
Message the client privately right away without responding inside the group chat.
Save the message to session notes so the client can review it later.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance, Standards 2.1–2.5), coaches safeguard confidential information and secure digital communications promptly. Option C is correct because alerting the client privately right away empowers the client to retract or mitigate the exposure immediately without amplifying the thread. Option D is clearly wrong because copying exposed third-party confidential data into coaching records increases privacy risk instead of mitigating the breach. Option A is a tricky distractor: messaging the whole group sounds proactive, yet triggers extra notifications and draws support staff's attention to sensitive details before the client can act. Option B is a tricky distractor (rigid deferral): waiting for the next session to discuss communication norms neglects urgent real-time data protection.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach who also runs an executive recruiting firm sees an active client as ideal for an open search mandate. How MUST the coach proceed?

options.text: Disclose the recruiting commission openly and pursue the placement alongside ongoing coaching sessions.
Refrain from recruiting an active client to protect coaching neutrality and role boundaries.
Explore the client's interest informally after a session while leaving the coaching intact.
Submit the client's profile to the hiring organization since the fit appears ideal.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest, Standard 3.1), coaches must recognize and manage conflicts of interest arising from dual roles and competing financial incentives. Option B is correct because declining to recruit an active client prevents an irreconcilable conflict between serving the client's unbiased agenda and earning a placement fee from a hiring employer. Option D is clearly wrong because forwarding a client's profile without consent breaches confidentiality and exploits the coaching relationship. Option A is a tricky distractor: disclosing the fee sounds transparent, yet disclosure alone does not resolve an active concurrent conflict of interest. Option C is a tricky distractor (wearing two hats): separating the pitch as an informal post-session chat still compromises role neutrality and client trust.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach notices feeling impatient with a client's indirect communication style shaped by cultural and generational norms. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Encourage the client to adopt a more direct communication style for greater clarity.
Share the feeling of impatience directly with the client to model authentic transparency.
Refer the client to another coach sharing their background to avoid cultural friction.
Examine personal assumptions through private reflection while respecting the client's communication norms.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Standard 3.5 on fairness and addressing biases), Section 4 (Standard 4.1 on cultural and relational power differentials), and Core Competency 4, coaches actively surface and manage their own biases rather than expecting clients to conform. Option D is correct because the coach takes ownership of personal biases through reflective practice while honoring the client's worldview. Option A is clearly wrong because pressuring the client toward directness imposes the coach's cultural norm. Option B is a tricky distractor: framing impatience as authentic transparency burdens the client with managing the coach's bias and erodes psychological safety. Option C is a tricky distractor (rigid over-correction): referring out immediately avoids doing essential self-reflection and unnecessarily disrupts the coaching partnership.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Mid-engagement, an executive client asks the coach for detailed guidance on cross-border corporate tax compliance restructuring. What should the coach do?

options.text: Note that tax guidance exceeds coaching scope and explore involving a tax specialist.
Provide brief general tax considerations first, then return to coaching the client's leadership goals.
Suspend all coaching sessions until the client settles the tax restructuring with advisors.
Outline standard cross-border tax restructuring strategies based on common multinational corporate practices.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice) and Code of Ethics Section 4 (recognizing competence limits and referring appropriately), coaches distinguish coaching from specialized technical consulting. Option A is correct because it clearly names the boundary around specialized tax advice and partners with the client on engaging an appropriate expert. Option D is clearly wrong because dispensing technical cross-border tax strategies violates scope of practice and competence boundaries. Option B is a tricky distractor (wearing two hats): offering only brief tax considerations before returning to coaching still blends unqualified technical advising into the session. Option C is a tricky distractor (rigid over-correction): halting the entire coaching engagement unnecessarily assumes coaching cannot support the client's broader leadership goals alongside specialist advice.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 4: Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: After an executive sponsor triples the coach's fee, the coach realizes they prepare noticeably more for that engagement than for individual clients. What should the coach do?

options.text: Maintain heavier preparation for the executive client because premium fees justify extra effort.
Cut back preparation for the executive engagement to keep effort identical across clients.
Reflect on the imbalance and recommit to consistent preparation quality for every client.
Increase individual client fees to match the preparation invested in the corporate contract.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 4 (Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value), coaches maintain the same high standard of professional quality and presence regardless of compensation level or fee structure. Option C is correct because the coach examines how fee disparity influenced professional habits and recommits to consistent preparation quality for all clients. Option A is clearly wrong because tying coaching diligence to fee size breaches Section 4 equity and consistency obligations. Option B is a tricky distractor (rigid over-correction): artificially reducing service to the executive client mistakes mechanical sameness for ethical consistency rather than elevating quality uniformly. Option D is a tricky distractor: raising individual fees to justify effort still treats coaching quality as conditional on price instead of an ethical baseline.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 5: Professional Integrity & Accountability
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach wants to showcase a client's glowing public LinkedIn comment about their coaching on the coach's website. How MUST the coach proceed?

Publish the comment with the client's name since it is already publicly visible.

Option D is clearly wrong because public visibility on LinkedIn does not grant commercial marketing rights or waive coaching privacy. Option A is a tricky distractor (diplomatic boundary erosion): anonymizing the quote seems protective, yet republishing client statements for marketing without consent bypasses client autonomy and risks indirect identification. Option C is a tricky distractor: notifying the client after publication sounds polite, yet acts unilaterally and pressures the client retroactively.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 5: Professional Integrity & Accountability
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach discovers a peer group colleague inaccurately lists the ICF Master Certified Coach credential on their website. What should the coach do first?

Address the discrepancy privately with the colleague first and encourage prompt correction.

Option A is clearly wrong because ignoring credential misrepresentation compromises integrity across the profession. Option B is a tricky distractor: warning the peer group appears protective of consumers, yet spreads unverified accusations instead of handling the issue constructively. Option C is a tricky distractor (rigid over-correction): filing an immediate formal complaint skips direct collegial dialogue when no imminent harm prevents speaking privately first.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 5: Professional Integrity & Accountability
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: After a client files a billing complaint with ICF Ethics Review, the coach prepares records containing several heated email exchanges. How MUST the coach proceed?

Option A is correct because providing complete, unaltered correspondence upholds honesty, accountability, and fair adjudication. Option D is clearly wrong because omitting relevant email evidence conceals material context from the formal review. Option B is a tricky distractor: offering a clean summary sounds organized and professional, yet selectively filters primary evidence needed by reviewers. Option C is a tricky distractor (rigid misapplication): invoking confidentiality to withhold heated billing replies during an active Ethical Conduct Review complaint brought by that same client misapplies Section 2 privacy to obstruct accountability.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Following a recent traffic collision, a client describes intrusive flashbacks and panic whenever approaching their car before work. What should the coach do?

Option A is clearly wrong because conducting exposure exercises attempts clinical trauma treatment outside coaching scope. Option B is a tricky distractor (wearing two hats / premature action): framing calming routines as confidence coaching sounds supportive, yet treats acute post-traumatic panic symptoms instead of referring to mental health care. Option D is a tricky distractor (rigid over-correction): abruptly terminating coaching without respectful discussion or referral options unnecessarily abandons the client rather than partnering thoughtfully.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: During a session, a VP asks the coach which executive equity-compensation structure retains senior software engineers best. How should the coach respond?

Option D is clearly wrong because recommending a specific vesting model puts the coach squarely in a technical consulting role. Option A is a tricky distractor (wearing two hats): offering brief industry compensation models before asking a coaching question still blends consulting without scope clarity. Option C is a tricky distractor (rigid over-correction): shutting down the topic entirely misses the opportunity to coach the VP on their strategic thinking and stakeholder engagement around compensation.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Advocacy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client feels passed over for promotion and asks the coach to write an endorsement memo to the leadership committee. What should the coach do?

Option A is clearly wrong because writing a persuasive promotion memo breaches confidentiality and turns coaching into advocacy. Option B is a tricky distractor (diplomatic boundary erosion): sending a neutral attendance or commitment note sounds harmless, yet still positions the coach as an organizational endorser. Option C is a tricky distractor: obtaining written consent before speaking with the chair satisfies permission mechanics, yet still involves the coach inappropriately in lobbying decision-makers.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client seeks coaching to stop checking work email at 3 a.m., noting that resisting triggers uncontrollable crying. What is the BEST action for the coach?

Option A is correct because the coach honors coaching scope without diagnosing and encourages appropriate therapy support. Option D is clearly wrong because issuing directive instructions breaches coaching autonomy while ignoring clinical distress. Option B is a tricky distractor (premature action / wrong scope): exploring bedtime routines sounds collaborative and coaching-aligned, yet treats potentially clinical distress as a routine productivity habit. Option C is a tricky distractor (empathy/analysis without scope check): probing deep 3 a.m. fears sounds exploratory, yet enters therapeutic emotional processing without addressing mental health referral.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 2: Embodies a Coaching Mindset
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: After a client brushes past an insight the coach found compelling, the coach feels frustrated and wants to restate it. What should the coach do?

Option D is a tricky distractor: disclosing personal frustration as feedback imposes the coach's emotional reaction onto the client.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 2: Embodies a Coaching Mindset
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach notices they have been offering different clients the same standard action prompts out of routine. What is the BEST step for the coach?

options.text: Compile a wider list of varied closing questions to rotate through future sessions.
Engage in reflective practice or supervision to renew curiosity around each client's context.

Option D is clearly wrong because relying on fixed templates disregards client uniqueness and stifles emergent partnering. Option A is a tricky distractor: building a larger question list sounds proactive, yet treats a curiosity and presence gap mechanically by rotating scripts rather than deepening mindset awareness. Option C is a tricky distractor (rigid over-correction): dropping action-planning prompts across sessions overreacts rather than restoring responsive, curious partnering.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 3: Establishes and Maintains Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: With ten minutes left in a session, a client raises an urgent workplace conflict they want to resolve before ending. How should the coach respond?

Ask what single action step the client can take immediately after leaving the session.
Invite the client to explain the conflict fully and summarize their main frustration quickly.

Option B is a tricky distractor (premature action): jumping straight to a quick action step bypasses re-contracting and rushes into Competency 8 before any exploration or awareness occurs. mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 4: Cultivates Trust and Safety
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: In their second session, a senior manager speaks guardedly, saying admitting self-doubt might "make me look incompetent as a leader." What is the BEST response for the coach?

Acknowledge how vulnerable doubt feels and affirm it signals thoughtful modern leadership.

Remind the manager that coaching cannot succeed unless they share personal doubts without hesitation.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under 2025 Core Competency 4 (Cultivates Trust and Safety), coaches honor the client's context and concerns while co-creating psychological safety without rescuing or pressuring. Option A is correct because it validates the manager's hesitation calmly and invites the client to define what supports candid openness. Option D is clearly wrong because demanding immediate vulnerability pressures the client and undermines safety. Option B is a tricky distractor (rescuing / reframing prematurely): acknowledging vulnerability before assuring them self-doubt signals strong leadership sounds encouraging, yet imposes the coach's reframing instead of exploring what safety the client needs. Option C is a tricky distractor (analysis / 'why' trap): asking 'why' they hold that belief pushes toward justification and defensiveness before trust is established.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 4: Cultivates Trust and Safety
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client tears up while discussing leaving their family business and quickly apologizes for losing composure. Which response BEST reflects coaching?

options.text: Suggest a short pause and pivot to reviewing next week's business transition timeline.
Acknowledge the emotion briefly and ask what practical step feels manageable right now.

Option C is correct because it removes shame around apologizing, affirms emotional safety, and uses intentional silence to let the client process. Option A is clearly wrong because pivoting straight to transition logistics avoids emotional reality. Option B is a tricky distractor (premature action): briefly acknowledging emotion before asking for a practical step rushes prematurely into Competency 8 problem-solving. Option D is a tricky distractor (analysis without presence): asking what belief triggered the reaction shifts immediately into cognitive analysis right when the client feels exposed, rather than grounding trust and space first.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 5: Maintains Presence
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Mid-session, a coach realizes they were planning their next question instead of hearing the client's last point. What is the BEST action for the coach?

Admit missing the last point candidly and ask the client to repeat it.
Ask an open question about their current feelings to rejoin the conversation smoothly.

Option B is correct because candidly owning the brief lapse and asking to hear the missed point prioritizes authentic listening and client respect over appearing polished. Option D is clearly wrong because asking the pre-planned question ignores what the client just shared and centers the coach's cleverness. Option A is a tricky distractor (diplomatic cover-up): summarizing an earlier point sounds seamless, yet masks inattention and skips the client's immediate words. Option C is a tricky distractor (faking presence): asking an open question about current feelings sounds coaching-oriented, yet conceals the lapse rather than genuinely hearing what was missed.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 5: Professional Integrity & Accountability
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A prospective business owner asks a coach to guarantee a 20% revenue increase within a 12-month coaching contract. How MUST the coach respond?

Include the 20% revenue increase as a guaranteed deliverable in the written coaching contract.
Decline to guarantee specific results and explain realistically what coaching can and cannot deliver.
Explain that formal guarantees are unavailable, though committed clients routinely achieve similar revenue gains.

Options A and D are tricky distractors: Option A uses an exploratory verb ('Explore...') yet leaves a prohibited guarantee open to negotiation; Option D politely refuses a written guarantee yet still breaches Section 5 by making unsubstantiated claims about typical client financial returns.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: An executive brings video of a struggling manager's presentation and asks the coach to evaluate whether the manager should be terminated. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Explain that evaluating staff is consulting and ask what criteria guide the executive's decision.
Review a short clip to share neutral impressions, then explore the executive's leadership options.
Redirect away from the manager entirely because termination decisions belong exclusively with human resources.
Assess the manager's recorded presentation and advise whether formal termination is warranted.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice), coaches clearly distinguish coaching from HR assessment and consulting, preserving client leadership ownership. Option A is correct because it clarifies that assessing a subordinate's performance sits outside coaching while inviting the executive to examine their own decision criteria. Option D is clearly wrong because evaluating the employee and recommending termination steps directly into consulting and managerial judgment. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B sounds balanced by reviewing only a short clip for neutral impressions before coaching, yet still mixes consulting assessment into the session; Option C rigidly over-applies boundaries by refusing to coach the executive around their own leadership decision-making.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Mentoring
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: During a session, a boutique agency owner asks the coach for warm introductions to corporate buyers from the coach's private network. How should the coach respond?

Send warm email introductions to two trusted corporate buyers right after the session ends.
End the coaching agreement because seeking client referrals creates an unmanageable conflict of interest.
Decline making introductions as outside coaching and explore how the owner can build relationships.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Mentoring) and Code of Ethics Section 3 (Conflicts of Interest), coaching develops client resourcefulness rather than brokering access through the coach's personal network, which belongs to mentoring or sponsorship and risks dual-role conflicts. Option D is correct because it maintains the role boundary cleanly and shifts focus to the owner's own networking strategy. Option B is clearly wrong because making the buyer introductions blends coaching with mentoring and creates reputational and relational conflicts. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A sounds strategic and exploratory yet still treats private introductions as a potential coaching deliverable; Option C over-corrects by terminating the coaching relationship rather than simply holding the boundary and coaching forward.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client briefly mentions feeling sad after a recent breakup, then shifts directly to exploring an upcoming career relocation decision. What should the coach do?

options.text: Clarify coaching boundaries respectfully and suggest working with a therapist on the breakup first.
Acknowledge the breakup briefly and follow the client's chosen focus on the career relocation.
Invite the client to process their breakup feelings first so emotion won't cloud choices.
Conduct a psychological screening to determine whether breakup distress impairs the client's decision judgment.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy), coaches distinguish ordinary, non-clinical human emotion from mental-health conditions requiring clinical referral, while Core Competencies 3 and 5 honor the client's chosen coaching agenda. Option B is correct because briefly acknowledging normal sadness shows humanity without pathologizing it, and follows the client's shift to their career relocation topic. Option D is clearly wrong because conducting a psychological screening falls strictly outside a coach's scope of practice. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A sounds ethically cautious yet misapplies therapy referral rules to ordinary sadness with no sign of impairment; Option C sounds empathetic and holistic yet redirects the client away from their chosen agenda into quasi-therapeutic emotional processing.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Management
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A sponsoring manager asks the coach to ensure their direct report completes mandatory compliance training every Friday. What is the BEST action for the coach?

Option C is correct because it establishes a clear boundary against acting as an operational manager while constructively educating the sponsor on proper coaching scope. Option B is clearly wrong because monitoring compliance and reporting missed deadlines assumes a supervisory role and violates confidentiality. Options A and D are tricky distractors: Option A uses a coaching-style question ('Ask...') yet adopts the manager's compliance-policing agenda without client ownership; Option D protects reporting confidentiality yet still accepts a managerial enforcement duty.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 3: Establishes and Maintains Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: At the start of Session 1, a client says, 'I just want to become a stronger leader.' What should the coach do first?

Outline a structured twelve-week leadership curriculum so the client has clear benchmarks early on.

Option A is correct because it invites the client to define 'stronger leader' in their own concrete terms and establish personally meaningful indicators of progress. Option D is clearly wrong because imposing a standardized twelve-week curriculum reflects directive training rather than client-partnered contracting. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B sounds forward-looking yet prematurely jumps into Competency 8 action planning before defining the goal; Option C sounds structured yet introduces the coach's predetermined competencies ('delegation or executive presence') instead of letting the client define what matters.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 3: Establishes and Maintains Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Halfway through a six-month engagement, a client's company is acquired, drastically shifting their role and daily responsibilities. What is the BEST next step for the coach?

options.text: Explore how the client can adapt their original goals to fit the buyer's expectations.
Close the coaching contract early because the original goals no longer fit this role.
Ask what immediate tactical actions the client needs to take under the new owners.
Invite the client to revisit the coaching agreement and redefine goals for current needs.

ai_rationale.explanation: Under 2025 Core Competency 3, specifically Sub-competency 3.12, the coach revisits the coaching agreement when needed to ensure the coaching approach continues to meet the client's needs. Option D is correct because major role and organizational disruption warrants pausing to re-contract around what serves the client now. Option B is clearly wrong because unilaterally ending the engagement misapplies agreement management instead of adapting through partnership. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A sounds adaptive yet keeps the client anchored to outdated goals and assumes external buyer priorities dictate the focus; Option C sounds supportive and practical yet leaps straight into Competency 8 tactical action without first realigning the overarching agreement.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 4: Cultivates Trust and Safety
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Mid-session, a client tells the coach bluntly, 'Your questions feel repetitive and aren't helping me today.' What is the BEST response for the coach?

Remind the client that effective coaching often requires repetitive questions to uncover deeper blind spots.

Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A sounds calm and transparent yet prioritizes justifying the coach's technique before adapting; Option C uses empathetic coaching verbs ('Acknowledge...', 'explore...') yet asks a defensive 'why' that puts the client on the spot to explain their critique rather than adjusting the session.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 5: Maintains Presence
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: While describing a difficult board decision, a client stops mid-sentence, looks toward the window, and pauses silently. What should the coach do?

Gently note the sudden pause and ask what feelings surfaced while looking away.
Pause briefly, then summarize their previous point to help them regain their thread.
Redirect the conversation back to the board decision so session time stays focused.
